extracted.intended_audience: humor scholars, linguists, discourse analysts, and computational humor researchers studying or analyzing verbal jokes
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH) to analyze or construct verbal jokes by identifying and evaluating six hierarchical knowledge resources that jointly produce humor. The framework is used for comparative analysis, taxonomy, and generation/evaluation of jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Opposition (SO)
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke must contain two opposing scripts. Listed as the most abstract knowledge resource inherited from Raskin's SSTH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether two opposed scripts are present (e.g., real/unreal, actual/non-actual, normal/abnormal, possible/impossible, sex/no-sex, money/no-money, life/death). Rubric question: 'Are there two opposed scripts?' Higher-level script opposition differences make jokes very different; scripts constrain lower-level choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Mechanism (LM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanism that resolves the incongruity between the opposed scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which LM resolves the incongruity (examples: false analogy, garden-path, reasoning from a false premise, juxtaposition, chiasmus, role exchange, role reversal, vacuous reversal, etc.). Attardo catalogs approximately 27 distinct LMs. Rubric question: 'What is the Logical Mechanism resolving them?' Use this to classify/compare how the switch between scripts is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (SI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'props' of the joke: objects, participants, instruments, activities; the setting and what's happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the Situation is specific and clear — identify setting, participants, instruments, and activities that instantiate the scripts and LM. Rubric question: 'Is the Situation specific and clear?' Situation elements constrain plausible LMs and language choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The butt of the joke (person, group, stereotype); optional in some jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether there is a Target and whether it is appropriate (e.g., ethnic groups, professions, individuals, stereotyped roles). Rubric question: 'Is the Target appropriate?' Note that Target may be absent in some jokes; presence affects social and ethical dimensions of the humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Strategy (NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the text is organized: the macro-structure or format of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the Narrative Strategy (e.g., simple narrative, dialogue, riddle, question-answer, expository) and evaluate fit between strategy and content. Rubric question: 'Does the Narrative Strategy fit (riddle vs. story vs. dialogue)?' NS choices constrain language-level realizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (LA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exact verbal expression: phonemic, morphemic, syntactic choices — the most concrete resource.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate language for tightness and choice: phonology, morphology, syntax, lexical items, timing, and wording. Rubric question: 'Is the Language tight and well-chosen?' Small changes at this level identify closely similar jokes; language realizes higher-level resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy & Substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle that higher-level resources determine and constrain lower-level ones; resources are hierarchical and substitutable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hierarchy to compare and assess joke similarity and generation: two jokes differing only in Language are very similar; two differing in Script Opposition are very different. When analyzing or creating jokes, consider top-down constraints (choose SO → LM → SI → TA → NS → LA) and permitted substitutions at each level. This principle informs evaluation (which differences matter more) and guides systematic variation for testing or generation.
